10058019:
Bill LD 2069: "An Act Designating July 21st as Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day"
Northeast Center for Occupational Health & Safety 1 Atwell Road Cooperstown, NY 13326
To the Committee Chair & Members:
We at the Northeast Center for Occupational Health & Safety strive to enhance the health and safety of agricultural, forestry and fishing (AgFF) workers throughout the Northeast. Our organization serves AgFF workers from Maine to Maryland, with much of our work with commercial fishermen taking place in Maine. We write in strong support of Bill LD 2069 to designate July 21st as Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day.
Commercial fishing, though one of the most dangerous occupations in the US, has shaped Maine's coastal identity for generations. Commercial fishermen are 13 times more likely to die on the job than the average worker, with East Coast fisheries reporting 288 fatalities between 2000 and 2019 [data from the National Institutes for Occupational Safety & Health].
Over the years, we have worked with many fishermen and unfortunately, many have shared stories about crew members or family who have died while fishing, and these events haunt these individuals for the rest of their lives. Many know someone who never came home. Our research also indicates that trauma is an issue in the industry and these effects can lead to issues with sleep, substance use disorder and other physical and mental health concerns. Just one year ago, two fishermen, father and son, Chet and Aaron Barrett were lost at sea in Maine when their vessel went down. But this isn't just a job to fishermen, it's a way of life passed down through generations with strong cultural ties to the working waterfront.
By designating a Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day, families, friends, fellow fishermen, and coastal communities that experience these losses so deeply, will have the opportunity to share memories of their loved ones and support each other in the healing process. However, it will also importantly underscore to the public the price these workers pay to ensure the rest of society has nutritious food on the table. This kind of recognition is essential in efforts to gather support for initiatives focused on crucial safety research, safety at sea training and search and rescue support to fishermen. We urge you to vote "yes" on Bill LD 2069.

Amanda Roome Northeast Center for Occupational Health & Safety LD 2069

10057582:
Written Testimony in Support of LD 2069
An Act Designating July 21st as Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day
Public Hearing January 21, 2026 at 10:00 a.m.
Submitted to: Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government Maine Legislature
My name is Ann-Marie R. Sokoloski, and I am writing in strong support of LD 2069, An Act Designating July 21st as Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day. While I am unable to attend the public hearing in person, I respectfully submit this written testimony to urge the Committee to support this important legislation.
Maine's commercial fishing industry is not only an economic driver it is a way of life, a heritage, and a community bound together by shared risk, responsibility, and resilience. Every person who works on the water understands that fishing is one of the most dangerous professions in our state. Loss is not abstract in our coastal communities; it is personal, remembered by name, boat, harbor, and family.
Designating July 21st as Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day gives our state a meaningful, permanent way to acknowledge those who have lost their lives while working to feed others and sustain Maine's maritime economy. It also provides space for families, fellow fishermen, and communities to grieve publicly, honor responsibly, and remember collectively.
This day is not about symbolism alone. It is about recognition of sacrifice, of risk, and of the quiet courage required to go back out after loss. It affirms that Maine sees its fishermen, values their labor, and remembers those who never made it home.
I also believe this designation supports broader goals of safety awareness, mental health visibility, and intergenerational understanding. When remembrance is recognized at the state level, it opens the door for education, reflection, and conversations that strengthen the fishing community rather than leaving grief unspoken.
I want to thank the sponsors of LD 2069, the many organizations and individuals who have worked to bring this bill forward. Their efforts reflect the best of Maine people showing up for one another and honoring those who can no longer speak for themselves.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Committee to vote Ought to Pass on LD 2069.

Thank you for your time, your consideration, and your service to the people of Maine.
Respectfully submitted, Ann-Marie R. Sokoloski Lubec, Maine
10057537:
Colleen Brown Whiting LD 2069
To the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government,
I am writing in support of LD 2069, An Act Designating July 21st as Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day.
Commercial fishing is not just an industry in Maine. It is a way of life, particularly in coastal and Downeast communities. I am the mother of a local fisherman, and the risks of this work are not abstract to me. They are real, daily concerns for families who send their loved ones out onto the water knowing that every trip carries danger.
Fishing is one of the most dangerous professions in the country, and many Maine families have lost fathers, sons, brothers, and crew members to the sea. In small towns, those losses are felt deeply and collectively. These are not statistics. They are empty seats at kitchen tables, children growing up without parents, and communities forever changed.
Designating a day of remembrance is a simple but meaningful way for the State of Maine to recognize the risks these men and women take and to honor those who have made the ultimate sacrifice. This bill does not create bureaucracy or cost. It creates recognition, respect, and visibility for an industry that has shaped Maine for generations.
I urge the committee to support LD 2069 and to give Maine's fishing families the acknowledgement they deserve.
Thank you for considering my testimony.
10057988:
21 January 2026
The Honorable Joseph Baldacci, Senate Chair The Honorable Suzanne Salisbury, House Chair Committee on State and Local Government Cross Building, Room 214 Augusta, ME. 04333
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, Honorable members of the Joint Committee on State and Local Government:
My name is Liz Michaud, a proud native of Downeast Maine, a University of Maine alumna, and someone deeply bonded to the commercial fishing community. I rise today in support of LD2069. Representative Tuell has already shared some of our family's story, so I'll keep it brief. I want to extend my heartfelt gratitude to Representative Tuell for his unwavering support and dedication to this cause. Ironically, it was exactly 30 months ago today, my 18year-old nephew tragically did not return from a day of lobster fishing. This devastating loss has left an indelible mark on our family, friends, and community. As Will mentioned, this tragedy inspired me to establish Green and White Hope Inc in April 2025. This Maine-based non-profit is dedicated to enhancing commercial fishing safety through education, technological advancements, and improved rescue and recovery efforts. However, that is not today's focus, my focus is to share why making July 21 an annual day for the state to honor and remember ALL of our lost commercial fishermen with "Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day" is right, just, and earned.
In 1880, the U.S. Fish Commission declared "Maine enjoys many advantages not possessed by other states for the prosecution of the fisheries." Maine has been a leader in the seafood economy since the 1800's. Today, the Maine fishermen continue to be the backbone of the seafood economy, contributing over 80% to the U.S. domestic lobster market (U.S. International Trade Commission, USITC, 2022) and employing over 33,000 marine living resource persons (Sea Maine Roadmap, 2019). This work is 40 times more fatal than the average U.S. job (NIOSH, Commercial Fishing Safety in the United States, 2025). Commercial fishing accidents happen and when they do, they generate significant publicity and calls to action, but this fades over time. The committee's support of "Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day" and hopefully the ultimate passing of this bill, will send a lasting message of appreciation, respect, and support to commercial fishermen, their families, and this heritage industry.
Last year, at my request, Governor Mills declared July 21, 2025, as the 1st "Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day." The request for this day was motivated by a need to honor the profound losses of four commercial fishermen Downeast in early 2025, as well as the many others who have perished across Maine, including Tylar, so their sacrifice is not forgotten. It also was meant to serve as a powerful call to action, urging us to visibly renew our commitment to enhancing safety and recovery efforts, with the ultimate goal of ensuring that every fisherman returns home.

The Governors' declaration was honored on that day with a heartfelt ceremony at the Lost Fishermen's Memorial in Lubec, ME. Nearly 200 attendees gathered, including families who had lost loved ones, legislators, dignitaries from the Department of Marine Resources, partner organizations in fishing safety, and members of the fishing community. For the first time, families who had experienced losses over the past two years came together, providing an incredible opportunity to support one another and keeping the memories of our loved ones alive. The event also showcased advancements in safety and wellness, sparking interest, hope, and momentum among attendees that future losses can be reduced. As we look to the future, I envision many Maine working waterfronts recognizing this day, creating a unified front to honor our lost fishermen with remembrance and hope. I respectfully ask for your support of LD2069, making July 21st annually "Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day".
Sincerely,
Liz Michaud Founder/President Green and White Hope, Inc

TESTIMONY OF Meredith Mendelson
Department of Marine Resources
The Department of Marine Resources (DMR) is testifying
In Support of
LD 2069 An Act Designating July 21" as Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day
Before the Committee on State and Local Government Sponsored by Representative Tuell Date of Hearing: January 21, 2026
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and
Local Government, my name is Meredith Mendelson, and I am the Deputy Commissioner of the Department of Marine Resources. l am testifying on behalf of the Department in support of LD 2069.
In 2025, at the request of Green and White Hope lnc., a nonprofit organization focused on saving lives
of commercial fishermen and bringing every fisherman home to their families and communities, Governor Mills issued a proclamation commemorating July 21, 2025 as Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day. The selection of that particular date was deliberate, as it was two years to the
day that the Michaud family lost Tylar Michaud, an 18-year-old lobsterman from Steuben.
LD 2069 would make observance of this day an annual occurrence, ensuring that there is ongoing opportunity to remember and reflect on those Maine fishermen who are lost at sea in pursuit of their
livelihoods. In doing so, it will also ensure that there is an ongoing opportunity to recognize the dangers associated with commercial fishing, and place renewed emphasis on efforts to mitigate those
risks.
The Department of Marine Resources strongly supports efforts to support a culture of safety for
commercial fishermen. For over 20 years, DMR has administered the Commercial Fishing Safety Council, which is charged with advising the Commissioner on fishing safety issues. More recently, DMR
supported legislation advanced by Representative Strout to create a Department administered Fund that can accept donations to improve safety in the commercial fishing industry and improve the department's ability to conduct search and rescue and recovery operations
In the aftermath of loss that too many Maine families and communities have experienced, it is
important to find ways to advance positive change. For this reason, the Department supports LD
2069.
Thank you for your consideration and I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.
10057636:
Monique Coombs Maine Coast Fishermen's Association LD 2069
Dear Members of the Committee on State and Local Government,
On behalf of the Maine Coast Fishermen's Association (MCFA), I write in strong support of the proposed proclamation recognizing July 21, 2025 as a day of remembrance for Maine fishermen who have lost their lives at sea.
Maine's working waterfronts are the backbone of our coastal communities and an essential part of our state's identity. Commercial fishing is not only one of Maine's most iconic industries, but one of its most demanding and dangerous. The men and women who fish our waters do so in an environment defined by uncertainty, weather that can turn in minutes, physically taxing labor, long hours, and ever-present risk. Too many Maine families and fishing communities have experienced the devastating loss of loved ones who did not return home. These losses ripple far beyond individual families, affecting entire towns.
I write also to remember one of our own. On January 23, 2020, Capt. Arnold "Joe" Nickerson IV, then President of MCFA's Board of Directors and a devoted advocate for fishermen across our state, died at sea along with his crew member, Christopher Pinkham, when his vessel the Hayley Ann capsized and sank. Joe was a fourth-generation Maine fisherman whose leadership, experience, and quiet strength deeply shaped our organization and the broader fishing community. His loss was a profound loss to families, friends, and all of us at MCFA.
Establishing a formal day of remembrance acknowledges that grief, honors the sacrifices made, and affirms that the lives lost to the sea are not forgotten. Importantly, this proclamation also serves as a call to action. By pairing remembrance with responsibility, Maine has an opportunity to recommit to the safety, health, and recovery of those who continue to work on the water. Organizations across the state that support fishing families and working waterfront communities stand ready to strengthen training, improve access to safety equipment and resources, and continue building a culture where prevention, preparedness, and safety are prioritized.
Recognizing July 21, 2025 as a day of remembrance is a meaningful and necessary step, one that honors the past, supports those who are still grieving, and reinforces our shared obligation to protect the future of Maine's fishing industry and the people who sustain it.
Thank you for your consideration and for your continued commitment to Maine's coastal communities, working waterfronts, and commercial fishermen.
Respectfully submitted, Monique Coombs Director of Community Programs Maine Coast Fishermen's Association
10057792:
Stephanie Chambers Addison LD 2069
Thank you for taking a moment to read my statement in favor of passing the LD2069 Bill. On January 18, 2025 our family's world as we knew it was changed forever. F/V Sudden Impact with Chet and Aaron Barrett on board was lost at sea. My sister, Melanie Barrett, lost Chet, her lifetime best friend and husband and Aaron, her only child; her son, her world was in that f/v. The father and son crew were moving their f/v and gear during scallop season. They had plans to be back at their homeport in South Addison well ahead of an impending storm system coming in overnight. When they became unreachable by radio, cell phone and were overdue at port; panic and chaos ensued. The next fifteen days were a blur yet every detail etched in our minds forever. Chet Barrett was recovered on February 2, 2025 however Aaron Barrett has not been recovered and his final resting place is at sea. Those days and events prompted the proposal and passing of the LD1708 Bill, thanks to Representative Tiffany Strout. Many of the residents in Maine either work on the water or have a family member dependent upon the sea for income: lobster fishing, shellfish diggers, scallop dragging, etc. The additional businesses in Maine that depend upon the fishermen for their work; such as boat builders, supply stores, trap makers, bait suppliers, etc. all support Maine economically. Each of these people are impacted by our fishermen; our fishermen who risk their lives from their first step off the dock until they have both feet back on land. In 2025, Washington County, Maine lost 4 fishermen. Chet Barrett; fishermen, husband, father, son, brother, uncle, friend to many. Aaron Barrett; fishermen, son, significant other, step-dad, nephew, cousin, friend to many. Jaxson Marston; fishermen, significant other, dad, son, grandson, uncle, friend to many. Alton Wallace; fishermen, husband, dad, son, brother, friend to many. Each of these men have a "story" and they deserve to be remembered for the life they lived, not just the tragedy that took their lives. On July 21, 2025 we attended the Fishermen's Remembrance Day in Lubec presented by Green Hope, Liz Michaud. We were in the early stages of grieving and had been advocating for Chet and Aaron Barretts' name to be engraved on the Lost Fishermen's Monument. The event was another step forward in the grieving process, we attended with the 3 other families that had lost their beloved fishermen in 2025. Additionally, we were able to meet the family of Tyler Michaud who was a young man lost to the sea in 2023. It was a day of reflection; a time of unity for our community. A day when we were all together, supporting one another, giving encouragement and sharing stories and tears. A day when complete strangers became lifelong friends. Living in a fishing community we need this remberance day; a dedicated day to stand side by side and reflect on our fishermen's life. In a generation of electronics, we need to teach our children, grandchildren and all the young fishing families that human contact and support is available when grieving. The loss of a fishermen has a ripple effect from the family, friends, fellow fishermen, throughout our small quaint towns, overflowing into the county and quickly spreading throughout Maine and from there out into the world. Speaking from the family perspective of 2 lost fishermen, the importance of a day dedicated to remembering our loved ones will let each of us know we are not alone. We will be acknowledging the daily risks of a fishermen and will be teaching the upcoming generations of fishermen that the State of Maine supports and respects their career choice. Please consider passing the LD2069 Bill; our lost fishermen deserve this recognition, these fishermen's spouses, children, grandchildren, extended family and friends deserve recognition for a life lost too soon to the sea. Thank you for your time and consideration of my testimony. Stephanie Chambers

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, Distinguished Colleagues on the State and Local Government Committee:
My name is Will Tuell. I represent central Washington County in the 132"" Maine Legislature, and am here today to present LD 2069, "An Act Designating July 21
as Maine Commercial Fishing Remembrance Day." I do so as a lifelong resident of Washington County who has watched scallopers, lobstermen, clam
diggers, and other commercial fishermen lose their lives while earning a living at
sea.
Some lost their lives in the dead of winter, navigating rough seas, howling winds, and driving rain and snow just to bring their catch, or their boat, safely to harbor. Some went out to dig clams on an early spring morning never to return home to their loved ones. And others got caught up in their boat's rigging and went overboard on placid summer days when their friends and neighbors were going to
Little League games, cookouts, or spending the weekend at camp.
Such was the case on July 21, 2023 when Tylar Michaud of Steuben went overboard while hauling lobster traps in the Moosabec region. Tylar was 18, a graduate of Sumner High School in the Hancock County town of Sullivan who graduated weeks before and had plans of attending school at Maine Maritime.

His aunt, Liz, is with us today on Zoom, and is the driving force behind this bill. She can tell her story better than I, but I can tell you that her family held an excruciating weeks-long search for Tylar's remains. They were joined by our Marine Patrol -- including Liz's son Alex who moved to Maine to become a Marine Patrol officer several years before -- first responders across the state, and
local fishermen who wanted closure.
Liz's mother, the Honorable Joyce Maker of Calais, who served in the House six years and two years in the Senate, is a close personal friend of mine. One of those friends you make up here that you just stay in touch with whether you're in office
or not. So I knew the anguish the family was going through and kept them in my
prayers throughout the whole ordeal.
House District 10

Tylar's story is not unique. Several years before, a young man who married a girl firom my neighborhood also went overboard. Last year, four commercial fishermen from Washington County lost their lives at sea.
In all cases, the tight knit communities of coastal Washington County came together, helped not just with search, rescue, and ultimately recovery efforts, but donated tens of thousands of dollars to help the families with lost loved ones carry
on.
That is right and just, but it is not enough. Liz channeled her grief into action and formed a nonprofit to advocate for fishermen's safety early last year known as Green and White Hope. Green and white were the colors ofTylar's buoys.
Last spring, Liz reached out to the Chief Executive's Office, asking if Governor Mills would proclaim July 21 Lost Fisherman's Remembrance Day. The Chief Executive did so, making Maine only the second state m the country to have done such a thing.
As admirable as Gov. Mills action was, Liz or someone else would have to come back every year for the same proclamation. When asked to attend a ceremony remembering those lost at sea Liz had organized for July 21,1 responded that I would be honored to do so and that I would also be willing to sponsor a bill to make the designation permanent.
Many of you likely read of the controversy that ceremony generated - not for anything Liz had done - but because two fishermen's names who lost their lives at sea were wrongfully left off a local monument m Lubec to honor all lost fishermen.
Liz and many others in the greater fishing community rallied for the lost fishermen, decisions were reversed, and the names of Chester and Aaron Barrett were added to the monument. Hundreds attended the ceremony in Lubec and paid their respects for all fishermen who lost their lives at sea.
I only bring this controversy up because it speaks to the importance of remembering our fishermen. If Liz had not approached the Governor, July 21 would have come and gone like any other day, yet because of it people were having difficult conversations about honoring those they had lost.
Those conversations while hard and sometimes negative, brought to the surface emotions that many in our small coastal communities buried - some for decades, others for generations. The need for a day for Mainers to honor our lost fishermen was, and is, more critical than ever.
House District 10

It's more critical because We can't have conversations about safety, well-being, and awareness without remembering those who were lost, saying to the
community that it is okay to grieve, to strive for something better, and to assure families that their loved one will always be remembered.
I am not proposing to make July 21 a paid state holiday. Much like your pancreatic
cancer designation bill and others, this is an opportunity to educate, observe, and
remember. I know Liz will have another ceremony this year, and maybe others up and down the coast will do the same. Those ceremonies will help communities ravaged by loss and despair heal, they Will help fishermen accept their own
mortality, and will help our state acknowledge that our billion dollar seafood industry is not just about dollars, cents, catch limits and quotas, it's about the
people that live a way of life that means a lot to our state.
I thank you for the opportunity to present this bill here today and ask for your unanimous support at work session, and would be happy to entertain any
